questions.q: What does perplexity measure, and how is it computed from the evaluation loop in this lesson?
options: The total number of parameters in the model; it is read directly from the checkpoint file
The model's effective 'confusion' over next-token choices, computed as exp(average cross-entropy loss) on held-out data
The number of training steps completed; it is just the step counter
The size of the vocabulary; it is always equal to vocab_size
questions.explain: Perplexity is exp(average cross-entropy loss) on a held-out set. It has an intuitive reading as the effective number of equally likely next-token choices the model is confused between -- lower is better.

questions.q: Why does the evaluate() function call model.eval() and wrap the loop in @torch.no_grad()?
options: eval() deletes the model's weights and no_grad() speeds up training
eval() turns off dropout so you measure real inference-time behavior, and no_grad() skips building the autograd graph, saving time and memory
Both calls are required before torch.save() can be used
eval() and no_grad() are interchangeable and either one alone is sufficient
questions.explain: model.eval() disables dropout (and similar training-only behavior) so the measured loss reflects real inference behavior. torch.no_grad() avoids building the autograd graph during evaluation, which is unnecessary and costly when you're not backpropagating.

questions.q: What is a known weakness of greedy decoding (always picking the argmax next token) compared to top-k or top-p sampling?
options: Greedy decoding is slower to compute than top-k or top-p
Greedy decoding often loops and repeats itself, since it always makes the same locally 'safest' choice
Greedy decoding cannot be implemented in PyTorch
Greedy decoding requires a larger vocabulary than top-k sampling
questions.explain: Because greedy decoding always picks the single highest-probability token, it has no mechanism to break out of repetitive patterns, and commonly produces looping or repeated text -- a classic symptom you should recognize when reading generated samples.

questions.q: During training, the loss keeps falling steadily while the validation loss flattens and then starts rising. What does this pattern indicate?
options: The model is underfitting and needs more parameters
This is the expected, healthy pattern for any training run
The model is overfitting -- memorizing training sequences rather than learning generalizable structure
There is a bug in the tokenizer's vocabulary
questions.explain: A falling training loss alongside a flattening or rising validation loss is the classic overfitting signature. For a tiny model on a small dataset, the fix is typically to stop training earlier, increase dropout, or add weight decay, not to add more parameters.

questions.q: When comparing a baseline run to an ablation (e.g. removing dropout), why does the lesson recommend changing only one variable at a time?
options: PyTorch only allows one hyperparameter to be changed per script
Changing multiple variables at once makes it impossible to attribute any observed difference in loss or perplexity to a specific cause
Multiple changes always cancel each other out numerically
It is a hard requirement of the DataLoader API
questions.explain: If you change the model size and the dropout rate in the same ablation, a difference in results could be caused by either change, so you can't draw a defensible conclusion. Changing one variable at a time keeps the comparison meaningful.
